paragraphs: Graph networks predict properties by passing information between connected nodes. Repeating this process should let distant parts of a graph influence one another, which matters when modeling complex systems. In practice, information can become too similar across nodes, be compressed through narrow communication paths, or fail to travel far enough. These problems are called oversmoothing, oversquashing, and underreaching.

The paper introduces a general framework that lets a message passing model learn how much propagation it needs and which messages to filter along the way. It places these choices within a variational inference framework. The central idea is to make depth and information flow adaptable, giving the model ways to address the competing difficulties involved in carrying information over long distances.

The authors support the approach with theoretical arguments and experiments on five node and graph prediction datasets. Their results indicate improved capture of long-range interactions and performance competitive with leading methods. The contribution is a learned strategy for mitigating these limitations, rather than a claim that adaptive propagation eliminates them altogether.
icml-2025-adaptive-message-passing-a-gen.tldr: Adaptive message passing learns propagation depth and message filtering to better capture long-range graph interactions.

paragraphs: Concept-based models make predictions through human-readable intermediate concepts, such as an object's color or pattern. This structure gives experts a direct way to intervene: correct a wrongly predicted concept and let the model update its final answer. The paper asks how well this mechanism works when inputs differ from the distribution encountered during training.

The authors identify a failure they call leakage poisoning. Information beyond the named concepts can influence the final prediction, and under distribution shifts this can prevent expert corrections from delivering the expected accuracy gains. Their proposed model, MixCEM, learns to use information missing from its concepts dynamically, exploiting that information only when it is in-distribution.

Experiments cover tasks with complete concept annotations and tasks without them. MixCEM improves accuracy over strong baselines for both familiar and out-of-distribution samples, with and without expert interventions. These findings connect interpretability to the behavior of information outside the explicit concepts: making concepts editable is more useful when the model also handles that additional information appropriately.
icml-2025-avoiding-leakage-poisoning-con.tldr: MixCEM controls its use of information beyond explicit concepts to improve predictions and expert interventions under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Wearable devices provide both low-level sensor readings and information about behavior. The paper focuses on the latter, arguing that behavioral signals can be especially informative because their quantities and timescales often match processes relevant to physiology. This motivates building foundation models directly around behavior, expanding the information used for health prediction.

The authors develop these models using more than 2.5 billion hours of wearable data from 162,000 people. They systematically examine model architectures and tokenization strategies, meaning the ways the data is divided into units the model can process. This design work addresses the particular structure of wearable behavioral information rather than assuming any foundation model design will serve equally well.

Evaluation spans 57 health-related tasks, including classifying individuals and predicting health states that change over time. The model performs strongly across these applications and particularly well on behavior-driven tasks such as sleep prediction. Combining its representations with representations of raw sensor data improves performance further, suggesting that the two sources provide complementary information for the evaluated health predictions.
icml-2025-beyond-sensor-data-foundation-.tldr: Foundation models trained on wearable behavioral data perform strongly across health prediction tasks and benefit further from raw sensor representations.

paragraphs: Some voice cloning defenses add adversarial perturbations to speech recordings so that cloning systems have difficulty reproducing the speaker's voice. This paper examines those defenses under threat models in which an attacker first tries to remove the protective changes. It systematically evaluates how well the protection survives such purification.

The authors find that existing purification methods can remove much of the perturbation while still leaving distortions in the internal features used by voice cloning models. Those remaining distortions continue to reduce cloning quality. Their proposed two-stage method first purifies the recording, then uses phoneme guidance to refine it toward the distribution of clean speech, addressing the residual mismatch.

In the reported experiments, this method is more effective at defeating voice cloning defenses than leading purification alternatives. The result identifies a specific weakness in perturbation-based protection: its apparent effectiveness can depend on distortions that a more targeted refinement process can reduce. The study therefore supports the need for more robust defenses against attackers who actively process protected recordings before cloning.
icml-2025-de-antifake-rethinking-the-pro.tldr: A two-stage purification method exposes weaknesses in protective audio perturbations by improving voice cloning after attempted defense removal.

paragraphs: Distributed learning asks multiple agents to improve a shared objective by exchanging information over a network. Communication can be costly, and different agents may hold very different data. This paper develops an ADMM-based approach that triggers communication only when needed and does not require similar data distributions across participating agents.

The authors analyze convergence in both convex and nonconvex settings, with accelerated convergence rates established in a convex setting. Their guarantees accommodate arbitrarily distinct local data distributions. They also characterize how communication failures affect the algorithm and demonstrate robustness to such failures, addressing another practical obstacle to coordinating learning across a network.

Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 report communication savings of at least 35% from the event-based strategy. They also show resilience to heterogeneous data and better performance than FedAvg, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, and FedADMM in the evaluated tasks. Together, the analysis and experiments support selective communication as a way to reduce network traffic while continuing to learn effectively from agents with different local datasets.
icml-2025-distributed-event-based-learni.tldr: Event-triggered distributed learning reduces communication while supporting convergence across agents with arbitrarily different local data distributions.

paragraphs: Turning everyday instructions into temporal logic helps people communicate precise requirements to robots and autonomous systems. This translation involves identifying the basic propositions mentioned in an instruction and assembling them into a formal expression. Existing methods struggle with grounding those propositions, resolving references to the same thing, and learning effectively from limited examples.

Grammar Forced Translation, or GraFT, reduces the choices a language model faces during both grounding and translation. Instead of selecting each output token from its entire vocabulary, the model chooses from a small set allowed at that step. The framework uses the properties of each subproblem to construct these restrictions, and the authors provide a theoretical explanation for why the smaller solution space enables more efficient learning.

On the CW, GLTL, and Navi benchmarks, GraFT improves average end-to-end translation accuracy by 5.49% and out-of-domain translation accuracy by 14.06% relative to leading approaches. These results support using formal task structure during generation to improve both complete translations and transfer beyond the evaluated training domains.
icml-2025-grammar-forced-translation-of-.tldr: GraFT improves natural-language-to-temporal-logic translation by restricting each generation step to a small set of valid tokens.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks need ways to connect information from distant parts of a graph. Graph state space models offer one route, but the paper identifies two shortcomings in existing approaches: some lose consistency under node relabeling, while others emphasize pairs of nodes rather than sequences. GRAMA addresses these issues through a learnable autoregressive moving average framework.

The method transforms static graph data into a sequential form so it can use the strengths of ARMA modeling. It preserves permutation equivariance: relabeling nodes produces the corresponding relabeling of outputs. A selective attention mechanism dynamically learns the ARMA coefficients, allowing long-range information propagation to adapt rather than relying entirely on fixed coefficients.

The authors establish theoretical connections between GRAMA and selective state space models to explain its ability to capture distant dependencies. Across 26 synthetic and real-world datasets, GRAMA consistently improves over the backbone models and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining sequence modeling with the structural consistency required for graph data.
icml-2025-graph-adaptive-autoregressive-.tldr: GRAMA uses adaptive ARMA sequence modeling to capture long-range graph dependencies while preserving permutation equivariance.

paragraphs: Comparing graphs is a basic step in tasks such as grouping similar networks, but doing so can become expensive for large collections. This paper introduces MMFD, a measure of graph dissimilarity derived by interpreting two adjacency matrices as kernel matrices associated with discrete distributions. It then compares the distributions to obtain a graph comparison.

The authors prove that MMFD is a pseudo-metric and show that its initially complicated definition has a simple closed-form solution. They build a clustering method, MMFD-KM, whose time and space requirements grow linearly with the number of graphs. They also introduce MFD, a generalization intended to use information in adjacency-matrix factors more effectively.

Experiments on simulated graphs illustrate how the proposed measures distinguish graphs. On real-world datasets, the methods outperform the evaluated competitors on three clustering metrics and time cost. The contribution combines a mathematically characterized dissimilarity measure with computational simplifications, making it useful for clustering large graph collections in the settings studied.
icml-2025-graph-minimum-factorization-di.tldr: MMFD provides a simply computed graph dissimilarity measure and supports clustering that scales linearly with the number of graphs.

paragraphs: Occam's razor favors simple explanations that fit the observations, a principle closely associated with generalization. Yet many machine learning objectives explicitly reward fit while encouraging simplicity only indirectly. This paper connects simplicity to in-context learning, where a sequence model learns from preceding observations during inference without a separate round of model training.

The key result links next-token prediction loss to prequential coding, a method of compressing data through sequential prediction. The authors show that minimizing this loss jointly minimizes prediction error and the complexity of the model implicitly learned from context. This gives the training objective a direct interpretation in terms of the tradeoff between explaining observations accurately and explaining them simply.

Theory and supporting experiments provide a normative account of in-context learning: an explanation of the objective it can be understood as pursuing. They also identify shortcomings in current approaches and suggest directions for improvement. The argument retains the underlying qualification that generalization guarantees require assumptions; it does not establish that simplicity guarantees generalization in every setting.
icml-2025-in-context-learning-and-occams.tldr: Next-token prediction connects in-context learning to Occam's razor by jointly penalizing error and the complexity of the implicitly learned model.

paragraphs: An evolving network can change not only in size but also in the patterns of connections it forms. This paper introduces Graphon Attachment Network Models, or GAN-M, to describe network formation with rich structural dependencies. Graphon functions determine attachment probabilities, giving the framework a temporal perspective alongside a flexible and interpretable description of connection structure.

The paper's main methodological contribution is a way to learn when that structure changes. It tracks counts of small graph patterns, including triangles and stars, as summaries of topology. The resulting signals are piecewise polynomial, and the authors introduce a statistic designed to identify changes in those signals. This connects observable substructure frequencies to changes in the evolving network.

The authors develop an efficient change-detection method and support it with theoretical guarantees. Numerical experiments across several network settings demonstrate its effectiveness. Together, the modeling framework and detection procedure provide a route for studying structural transitions through small-pattern counts, with the reported results highlighting its potential for dynamic network analysis.
icml-2025-learning-changes-in-graphon-at.tldr: GAN-M models evolving network attachment and detects structural changes through signals built from small-subgraph counts.

paragraphs: Learning to coordinate large networks of agents is difficult because both computation and mathematical analysis become demanding. Mean field methods offer efficient approaches for dense and moderately sparse networks, but realistic networks with fewer connections remain challenging. This paper develops a mean field control model specifically aimed at that sparser regime.

The model draws on local weak convergence and includes sparse networks such as power law networks with coefficients above two. Alongside theoretical analysis, the authors design scalable learning algorithms for graph sequences with a finite first moment. This condition identifies the class their algorithms address and is part of the contribution's stated scope.

The authors compare their approach with methods based on Lp graphons and graphexes across examples involving synthetic and real-world networks. Their method performs better in many examples and on various networks. These findings support the value of designing the approximation around sparse network structure, extending efficient learning tools to an important class of multi-agent problems that earlier approaches have struggled to handle.
icml-2025-learning-mean-field-control-on.tldr: A mean field control model tailored to sparse graphs enables scalable learning and improves over existing methods in many evaluated networks.

paragraphs: Low-Rank Adaptation reduces how many parameters must be trained when adapting a model, but its performance often trails full fine-tuning. Existing improvements use fixed subsets from singular value decomposition to initialize adaptation or introduce multiple experts. Combining those ideas is difficult because the weights and optimization dynamics can become misaligned.

GOAT addresses both the selection of prior knowledge and the alignment of training. It uses an SVD-structured mixture of experts to adaptively incorporate relevant information from pretrained weights. It also derives a theoretical scaling factor that aligns optimization with a fully fine-tuned mixture of experts. The paper shows that appropriate scaling can improve LoRA expert models without changing their architecture or training algorithms.

Experiments cover 25 datasets spanning language understanding, commonsense reasoning, image classification, and language generation. The authors report state-of-the-art performance and a closing of the gap with full fine-tuning. The findings emphasize that parameter-efficient adaptation depends on both which pretrained information is used and how the resulting updates are scaled.
icml-2025-make-lora-great-again-boosting.tldr: GOAT combines adaptive SVD-based experts with theoretically motivated scaling to improve LoRA and close its performance gap with full fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Maximum coverage asks which k subsets together contain the largest number of distinct items. This paper studies the problem when subset membership changes through a stream of individual insertions and deletions. That turnstile setting requires an algorithm to maintain useful information as memberships change, including when previously observed items are removed.

The authors present the first maximum coverage algorithm for this streaming model, with update time polynomial in the logarithm of the universe size. They also develop streaming algorithms for targeted and general fingerprinting, where the aim is to identify features that create the greatest risk of re-identifying people in a dataset. A further contribution estimates the complement of the pth frequency moment of a vector for p at least two.

Empirical evaluation of the fingerprinting algorithms reports speedups of up to 210 times over prior work. This supports their practicality for the evaluated risk-management computations. The paper links efficient handling of changing set memberships with the assessment of which combinations of dataset features create identification risk.
icml-2025-maximum-coverage-in-turnstile-.tldr: New turnstile streaming algorithms support maximum coverage and re-identification risk analysis, with fingerprinting speedups reaching 210 times in evaluation.

paragraphs: Specialized models can handle individual chest X-ray interpretation tasks, but using them in isolation limits how they can contribute to more complex medical questions. MedRAX brings chest X-ray analysis tools and multimodal language models together in a single agent framework. Its purpose is to coordinate existing capabilities when a query requires more than one kind of analysis.

The agent dynamically uses the integrated models to address medical queries without requiring additional training. This makes coordination a central part of the contribution: the framework can draw on specialized analysis and language-based reasoning within the same process. The paper positions this integration as a step toward making separate chest X-ray tools more useful together.

The authors also introduce ChestAgentBench, containing 2,500 complex medical queries across seven categories. In their experiments, MedRAX achieves state-of-the-art performance against both open-source and proprietary models. These findings establish strong benchmark performance for the integrated agent and support further progress toward practical automated chest X-ray interpretation, which the paper presents as the broader deployment goal.
icml-2025-medrax-medical-reasoning-agent.tldr: MedRAX coordinates chest X-ray tools and multimodal language models to answer complex medical queries without additional training.

paragraphs: Long robotic manipulation tasks are difficult to learn when rewards provide little feedback along the way. A robot must explore many possible actions before discovering a successful sequence, while manually designing detailed rewards is itself challenging. This paper uses the fact that these tasks often consist of several stages that can be treated as manageable subgoals.

The proposed DEMO³ framework combines demonstrations with reinforcement learning from visual inputs. It brings together learned dense rewards for multiple stages, a training scheme with two phases, and world model learning. These components use the task's staged structure to reduce the exploration challenge and make learning more efficient despite the original rewards being sparse.

Evaluation covers 16 sparse-reward tasks across four domains, including difficult humanoid visual control tasks, with as few as five demonstrations. The authors report an average data-efficiency improvement of 40% over leading approaches and 70% on particularly difficult tasks. These results support using demonstrations throughout reward, policy, and world model learning to help solve extended manipulation sequences.
icml-2025-multi-stage-manipulation-with-.tldr: DEMO³ combines demonstrations, staged reward learning, and world models to improve data efficiency on long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies assistance games in which a human and an AI have incomplete observations. It asks whether an assistant can have an incentive to alter what the human observes. The authors prove that some optimal assistants must take observation-interfering actions, even with an optimal human and otherwise-equivalent noninterfering actions available.

That result appears to conflict with the principle that perfect information has nonnegative value in single-agent decisions. The authors resolve the tension by defining interference over whole policies rather than isolated actions, extending the information-value perspective to cooperation. This distinction matters because judging an individual action and judging an entire decision strategy need not yield the same conclusion.

Other incentives depend on human behavior. With a human focused on immediate outcomes, interference may help query preferences; this particular incentive disappears with optimal human play or a preference-communication channel. A Boltzmann model of irrationality can also create interference incentives. An experimental model explores practical tradeoffs, showing why the source of an incentive matters when interpreting or addressing it.
icml-2025-observation-interference-in-pa.tldr: Partially observable assistance games reveal several distinct incentives for AI assistants to interfere with human observations, including some involving optimal humans.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning for on-device language models must accommodate users with different data and devices with different computational resources. Limited local data also makes personalization vulnerable to overfitting. CoMiGS addresses these challenges through a mixture of shared generalist experts and local specialist experts, combining broadly useful knowledge with information specific to each user.

The number of local specialists can vary with a user's resources, while generalists are shared across users. A router decides how to use the experts. The authors formulate training as a bi-level optimization problem, optimizing the router on a separate validation set to align it with the target distribution. They solve the objective through alternating minimization and provide theoretical analysis of this procedure.

Experiments show that CoMiGS balances general and personalized knowledge for individual token predictions. The shared generalists have a regularizing effect that helps resist overfitting, while specialists adapt to local data. The framework therefore connects resource-aware personalization with privacy-preserving local expertise, addressing both data and computational differences within one collaborative modeling approach.
icml-2025-on-device-collaborative-langua.tldr: CoMiGS combines shared generalists with resource-dependent local specialists to support personalized, privacy-preserving language modeling across heterogeneous devices.

paragraphs: Language agents can struggle with tasks that require many coordinated steps. Separating high-level planning from detailed execution helps organize that work, but a language model still needs to learn how to produce useful plans. Plan-and-Act addresses both the division of responsibilities and the training data needed to improve planning.

The framework uses a Planner to produce structured plans for a user's goal and an Executor to convert those plans into actions suited to the environment. To train the Planner, the authors generate synthetic data by annotating ground-truth trajectories with feasible plans. They augment these annotations with diverse examples intended to improve generalization, providing a scalable way to teach planning from action sequences.

Evaluation uses web navigation as a representative setting for long-horizon tasks. The system achieves a reported state-of-the-art success rate of 57.58% on WebArena-Lite and a text-only state-of-the-art rate of 81.36% on WebVoyager. These results support explicitly training planning capability alongside an architecture that separates goal-level organization from environment-specific execution.
icml-2025-plan-and-act-improving-plannin.tldr: Plan-and-Act trains a dedicated planner with synthetic plan annotations and pairs it with an executor to improve long-horizon web navigation.

paragraphs: Statistical evaluation can combine many machine-generated labels with a smaller collection of high-quality human labels. Prediction Powered Inference, or PPI, provides a framework for using these sources to obtain unbiased estimates with low variance. This paper examines what happens when the supply of trustworthy labels is especially small, a setting where obtaining more may be costly.

The authors find that PPI++, an existing method, can perform worse than classical inference in this few-label regime. They explain the problem by relating PPI++ to ordinary least squares regression, which can also have high variance when fitted from small samples. This connection turns a surprising failure into a regression problem that can be analyzed more directly.

Building on that view, the paper proposes two PPI-based techniques that use robust regressors to produce lower-variance estimators when labels are scarce. The contribution is both diagnostic and methodological: it explains why adding pseudo-labeled information does not automatically improve estimation and uses that explanation to design techniques better suited to limited high-quality supervision.
icml-2025-regression-for-the-mean-auto-e.tldr: A regression view explains PPI++ failures with very few labels and motivates two robust-regression techniques with lower estimator variance.

paragraphs: Quantum control seeks control signals that produce desired dynamics in quantum systems. Complex systems are difficult to optimize, especially when dissipation and noise affect their behavior. This paper develops a reinforcement learning algorithm that narrows its search using physical knowledge about both the desired dynamics and the signals that can realistically be applied.

The constraints incorporate prior information about the timescales on which quantum states should evolve and practical limits on control signals. The authors find that these restrictions improve solution quality and computational scalability. Their evaluation includes three quantum systems and accounts for complications from dissipation and perturbations of the control signal.

Across all three evaluated systems, the reported fidelities exceed 0.999, with better fidelity and robustness than previous methods. The approach also improves resistance to time-dependent perturbations and experimental imperfections. Finally, the authors show that incorporating feedback over multiple steps can produce solutions robust to strong perturbations. The results support using physical constraints to guide learning toward effective control strategies.
icml-2025-reinforcement-learning-for-qua.tldr: Physics-constrained reinforcement learning improves quantum control fidelity and robustness by incorporating timescale priors and realistic signal limits.

paragraphs: Autonomous driving planners must generate suitable trajectories while responding quickly to changing situations. Rule-based methods offer efficiency, while learned methods can generalize more broadly but face challenges in runtime and interpretability. The paper focuses on combining their strengths, particularly for uncommon scenarios that are difficult for either approach to handle alone.

SAH-Drive integrates a lightweight rule-based planner with a more comprehensive learning-based planner. A dual-timescale decision neuron determines the final trajectory, drawing inspiration from human driving behavior. The system also includes a regulator for the number of diffusion proposals and a trajectory fusion module, which are introduced to improve computational efficiency and robustness.

Experiments report improved generalization and state-of-the-art performance on interPlan, while maintaining computational efficiency without substantial additional runtime. These findings support the proposed hybrid design for the evaluated closed-loop planning setting. The contribution lies in coordinating the two planning approaches and managing their computational demands, so that greater planning capability can be obtained without a large increase in execution time.
icml-2025-sah-drive-a-scenario-aware-hyb.tldr: SAH-Drive coordinates rule-based and learned planners to improve driving generalization without substantial additional runtime in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: Training planners for many tasks often requires expert demonstrations or carefully designed reward labels. Both can demand considerable human effort. This paper asks whether broad collections of suboptimal trajectories, gathered without a specific task objective, can instead provide a useful starting point for a planner that later adapts quickly.

SODP uses two stages. First, it trains a diffusion planner to model a broad distribution of trajectories across tasks, extracting general planning capability from data that need not be expert quality. Second, it fine-tunes the planner using reinforcement learning and rewards for a particular downstream task. This adaptation aims to produce action sequences with higher returns for that task.

Experiments in multi-task domains including Meta-World and Adroit show better performance than leading methods with only a small amount of reward-guided fine-tuning data. The approach separates broad trajectory learning from targeted improvement, making suboptimal data useful for pretraining. Task-specific rewards remain part of the fine-tuning stage, where they guide the general planner toward the desired behavior.
icml-2025-task-agnostic-pre-training-and.tldr: SODP pretrains a diffusion planner on broad suboptimal trajectories, then uses limited reward-guided fine-tuning to adapt it to specific tasks.

paragraphs: Compositionality concerns how familiar parts can combine into new wholes. In AI, this idea motivates systems that handle new combinations of known concepts. Although the intuition is influential, the paper argues that satisfying formal definitions have been missing, making it difficult to express precisely what makes a representation compositional.

The authors propose a quantitative definition called representational compositionality, grounded in algorithmic information theory. Its central requirement combines two properties: the representation must be expressive, and it must be describable as a simple function of its parts. Expressiveness captures the ability to represent information, while the simple description captures the structured relationship between the whole and its components.

The authors validate the definition on real and synthetic data and show how it brings together different intuitions from AI and cognitive science. The main contribution is a formal framework for describing and assessing representations. They also propose that this foundation could inspire future models of compositional thought, presenting that prospect as a research direction rather than an already demonstrated modeling outcome.
icml-2025-towards-a-formal-theory-of-rep.tldr: Representational compositionality formalizes the idea that useful representations should be expressive yet describable as simple functions of their parts.

paragraphs: Unlearning aims to remove the influence of unwanted information from a language model. However, existing methods can leave models vulnerable to relearning attacks, where a small number of examples restores information that was supposed to be removed. This paper investigates how to make unlearning more resistant to that subsequent training.

The authors establish a connection between robust unlearning and sharpness-aware minimization through a shared robust optimization framework. They draw an analogy with adversarial training and analyze the role of smoothness optimization in reducing vulnerability to relearning. This analysis motivates examining additional smoothing strategies, broadening the approach beyond a single optimization method.

Experiments on benchmarks including WMDP and MUSE show that sharpness-aware minimization and other smoothness-based approaches consistently improve resistance to relearning attacks. The authors also find benefits against input-level jailbreaking attacks. The findings support smoothness as a useful design principle for more robust unlearning, with the demonstrated outcome being improved resistance across the evaluated attacks rather than a guarantee of irreversible forgetting.
icml-2025-towards-llm-unlearning-resilie.tldr: Smoothness-based optimization makes language-model unlearning more resistant to relearning attacks and also helps against evaluated jailbreaks.

paragraphs: Designing difficult video question-answering benchmarks usually relies on human judgments about which questions require demanding reasoning. This paper experimentally finds that people struggle to predict what machine learning models will find difficult. It proposes estimating question complexity automatically using code generated for visual question answering.

The approach treats the complexity of that generated code as a proxy for question difficulty. The authors show that this measure correlates significantly better with model performance than human estimates do. They also develop an algorithm that identifies fine-grained primitives associated with the hardest questions for a chosen set of models, allowing the analysis to be applied to new approaches.

The method is then extended from analyzing questions to generating complex ones. This produces a benchmark reported to be 1.9 times harder than NExT-QA. The contribution connects benchmark construction to observed model difficulty: generated programs provide a way to examine the operations behind challenging questions and use that evidence to build a more demanding evaluation.
icml-2025-understanding-complexity-in-vi.tldr: Generated visual-program complexity predicts VideoQA difficulty better than human estimates and supports automatic creation of harder questions.
